scenario.name: NSA/CISA Kubernetes Guide & CNCF Falco DFIR — Kubernetes Audit Log Privileged Pod & hostPath Container Escape
scenario.overview: Imagine a guarded container warehouse where a rogue worker first asks the front-desk policy book what rooms their badge can unlock, then orders a brand-new privileged inspection booth with its back door hinged directly onto the warehouse master floor, and finally steps straight out of that booth into the warehouse chief control room while a kernel-level floor sensor sounds an immediate alarm. In this scenario (T1613, NSA/CISA Kubernetes Guide & CNCF Falco DFIR, Kubernetes Audit Log Privileged Pod & hostPath Container Escape), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: serviceAccount RBAC SelfSubjectRulesReview, then privileged Pod Creation with hostPID: true, then host Namespace Escape via nsenter -t 1 -m -u. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering ServiceAccount RBAC SelfSubjectRulesReview, then Privileged Pod Creation with hostPID: true, then Host Namespace Escape via nsenter -t 1 -m -u, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection pivots on Auditd Event 201 correlated across the documented kill chain.

stages.title: Stage 3: Host Namespace Escape via nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n & Falco eBPF Alert
stages.subtitle: Privilege Escalation (T1611 - Escape to Host via nsenter setns Syscall)
stages.description: Stepping inside the newly launched breakout booth, the intruder flips the namespace master switch straight into the underlying node main supervisor process, triggering an unmistakable kernel-level breakout siren. Because hostPID: true exposes the worker node PID 1 (/proc/1/ns/*) inside the container and privileged: true grants CAP_SYS_ADMIN, the actor executes nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid to transition into the underlying worker node host namespaces, immediately triggering a CNCF Falco eBPF alert on setns() syscall execution from a container cgroup (logged in Linux Audit Event 308 with RuntimeSensor=CNCF Falco eBPF / Linux Auditd, Syscall=308 , sys_setns joining host PID 1 namespaces, ContainerId=8f19c2a04b12 , k8s.pod.name=node-debug-helper, EscapedTarget=Worker Node Host OS , PID 1 Namespace so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Container Process: nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- /bin/bash (which invokes nsenter , targeting /proc/1/ns/* or chroot /host inside a privileged container to attach the process to the underlying Linux node's root PI so that breaks out of container cgroup/namespace isolation , T1611 during "Host Namespace Escape via nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n & Falco eBPF Alert" to gain unrestricted root execution on the underlying Kubernetes worker node and access host credentials , kubelet / systemd). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- /bin/bash / ⇠#3 ACK 308) from Node ③ (#3 kube-apiserver (audit.log)) to Node ④ (#4 Privileged Pod (hostPath: /)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Worker Node Host PID 1 (nsenter)).

steps.plainTitle: Host Namespace Escape via nsenter -t 1 -m -u -i -n & Falco eBPF Alert
steps.storyAnalogy: Stepping inside the newly launched breakout booth, the intruder flips the namespace master switch straight into the underlying node main supervisor process, triggering an unmistakable kernel-level breakout siren.
